  "text": "When the old train station reopened as a library, June volunteered to sort the books left behind by its previous tenants. Most were water-damaged timetables and faded travel guides, but one afternoon she found a small red notebook tucked beneath a loose floorboard.

June remembered the day. Her father had been delayed, and she had sat on a bench with an old man who claimed he was waiting for a train to a place that no longer appeared on the maps. She had forgotten him almost entirely.

The next morning, she asked the station’s retired ticket clerk about the notebook. He studied the handwriting and smiled. “That was Mr. Vale,” he said. “He kept track of people because he was afraid the station would forget them.”

June placed the notebook in a glass case near the entrance, with a fresh page beside it. Visitors began adding their own small observations: a child asleep on a suitcase, a couple sharing an umbrella, a dog refusing to board.

Soon, the library held more than books. It held traces of arrivals and departures, of ordinary moments someone had thought worth saving. June added one final note: “An old station learning how to welcome people again.”"
